platforms.label: Unified memory (Apple Silicon)
platforms.pickerLabel: Apple Silicon — graphics built into the chip
platforms.blurb: macOS lets the GPU wire down about 75% of unified memory, and llama.cpp treats that as the limit. The CPU shares that same memory rather than adding a second pool, so splitting a model between the two — which is how a machine with a graphics card runs something oversized — gains almost nothing here and costs speed. Raising the cap is the lever on these machines.

ceiling.note: macOS exposes recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize at roughly 75% of unified memory and llama.cpp treats it as a hard ceiling. Measured at 26,800,603,136 bytes (24.96 GiB) on a 32GB M2 Max, which is 78% rather than exactly 75. The 75% used here is an ASSUMPTION applied to every Apple machine, and the real figure varies by model and capacity — reported anywhere from two thirds to about three quarters. It does not have to be assumed: Metal answers the question directly, and MLX exposes the answer as mx.device_info()['max_recommended_working_set_size']. That is the number to plan against on any specific machine, and it beats every percentage on this page including ours.

raise.note: How far this site OFFERS the cap raised, which is not the same as how far it is safe to raise it — nobody can tell you that. Apple documents iogpu.wired_limit_mb nowhere, so there is no official guidance and this project is not an authority on what your machine survives. The offer stops at RAM minus the OS reserve, the same figure the budget itself uses. That is deliberate: raising the limit grants a PERMISSION, it does not free memory. macOS and your other apps still draw on the same pool and llama.cpp has no view of them, so a limit set above what the system needs is a number the machine will not honour in practice. An earlier version offered more than the budget would ever spend, from a second uncited reserve; that arithmetic never bound at any capacity and has been removed. publishedReserveGb is what a cited source recommends holding back, kept for comparison — the offer here is currently more conservative than it at every capacity. Whatever you set, it is a runtime sysctl: it reverts on reboot, so the worst case is restarting rather than a broken machine.

reserve.note: Left for macOS and your other apps. Proportional because a fixed number is wrong at both ends of the range: macOS idles near 3-4GB on an 8GB machine and comfortably uses 8-10GB on a 32GB one with a browser open. Independently corroborated: oMLX, a production Apple Silicon inference server, holds back 6 GiB by default on the same class of machine where this reserve holds back 6.4GB. Two implementations arriving at the same figure from different directions is the closest thing to evidence this number has.

advice.label: Raise the GPU memory limit
advice.newbieExplainer: By default macOS lets the GPU claim about 75% of your memory, and llama.cpp will not load a model larger than that even when you have RAM to spare. That 75% is this site's assumption, not your machine's answer — Metal will tell you the real number, and two lines of Python get it: mx.device_info()['max_recommended_working_set_size']. You can also raise the cap. How far is genuinely unsettled: Apple documents the setting nowhere, so nobody — this site included — can tell you what your machine will survive. Raise it in steps and leave the system several gigabytes. Note the failure mode is not a clean error: a graphics card that runs out of memory stops the program and leaves the machine working, whereas an over-committed Mac pushes the pressure into the memory compressor and then into swap, so the symptom is a machine that goes slow rather than a model that refuses to load. The good news is the shape of it: this is a runtime setting that reverts when you reboot, so treat it as a session. Raise it, run the model, put it back. The worst case is a restart.
advice.caveat: Reverts on reboot, so nothing here is permanent unless you make it so with a login script — which is worth avoiding, since it would give up the headroom on every boot including the ones where you are not running a model. The cap is a permission, not spare memory: set it past what the system needs and the machine swaps and stutters. And your runtime may not use it. Serving engines apply their own memory ceiling, often lower: oMLX takes min(RAM minus its own reserve, the sysctl, Metal's hint), so on a 32GB machine its 6 GiB reserve binds at 26GB and raising the sysctl above that changes nothing at all. If a raise appears to do nothing, check what your runtime thinks its ceiling is before raising it further.

platforms.label: Unified memory — AMD (Strix Halo)
platforms.pickerLabel: AMD Strix Halo — graphics built into the chip
platforms.blurb: Ryzen AI Max+ APUs share one memory pool, but the GPU's slice is fixed in UEFI at boot rather than allocated on demand.

ceiling.note: Windows allows up to 96GB of a 128GB machine to be allocated as VRAM — exactly three quarters. Linux with amdgpu reaches roughly 110-120GB. The split is set in UEFI at boot, not at runtime, so it is a reboot away rather than a command away.

raise.note: Strix Halo's split is set in UEFI at boot, not by a running command, so this is a reboot away rather than a keystroke away — and unlike the macOS setting, a bad value does not fix itself when you restart. The offer stops at RAM minus the OS reserve, the same figure the budget uses. What IS sourced for this hardware: Windows hands the GPU up to 96GB of a 128GB machine, and Linux with amdgpu reaches roughly 110-120GB. The published figure recorded here is the conservative end of the Linux range, and only for 128GB, because that is the only capacity the source names.

reserve.note: Lower than a general-purpose desktop: these are bought to run models, so less is held back for everything else.

advice.label: Raise the GPU memory allocation
advice.newbieExplainer: On Strix Halo the graphics memory is carved out of system RAM in UEFI, and the default share is smaller than the machine can give. Raise the UMA Frame Buffer / VRAM setting in firmware and reboot. Running Linux lifts the ceiling further still — amdgpu will hand the GPU roughly 110-120GB of a 128GB machine where Windows stops at 96GB.
advice.caveat: Set in firmware at boot, so it needs a reboot to change and another to undo, and whatever you allocate is unavailable to the rest of the system. Unlike the macOS setting, a bad value here does not fix itself when you restart.

platforms.label: Unified memory — NVIDIA (DGX Spark)
platforms.pickerLabel: NVIDIA DGX Spark — graphics built into the chip
platforms.blurb: GB10 Grace Blackwell shares one coherent pool between CPU and GPU with no fixed split — the model, the KV cache, the OS and the display all draw from the same 128GB.

ceiling.note: No GPU-specific cap to raise: allocation is dynamic. What limits you is simply what the rest of the system is using.

reserve.note: A dedicated AI appliance, so less is reserved than on a general-purpose desktop.

platforms.label: Discrete GPU (NVIDIA / AMD)
platforms.pickerLabel: A separate graphics card (NVIDIA / AMD / Intel) + your CPU
platforms.blurb: The model runs fastest entirely inside the card's own memory. Anything larger still runs: the card takes what it holds and your CPU runs the remaining layers out of system RAM, at the speed of that memory rather than the card's.

ceiling.note: About 1GB of VRAM is already spoken for by the desktop and display buffers.

reserve.note: Applies only to the system RAM your CPU runs offloaded layers from, not to the card's memory.

offload.note: Layers the card cannot hold stay in system RAM and are run there by the CPU — they are not streamed to the card. Both processors work on every token, and the CPU's share, being much the slower of the two, sets the pace.

platforms.label: CPU only (no GPU acceleration)
platforms.pickerLabel: No graphics card — your CPU does all of it
platforms.blurb: Everything runs on the processor. It works and it is slow — expect a few tokens per second on anything above 8B.

ceiling.note: No graphics cap applies; system RAM minus the reserve is the whole budget, and the speed of that RAM is the whole of the speed.

reserve.note: Left for the OS and other applications.

thresholds.note: A fit is tight when it passes either test. Percentage alone is too loose on a 128GB machine and too strict on an 8GB one, so the absolute floor scales with the machine. Splitting a model between the card and the CPU is only offered while at least this share still sits on the card: below roughly half, the CPU is running most of the model and the card has stopped being the reason the machine is quick. Held at a half deliberately — it is a conservative line, not a physical one, and moving it should be argued from measurements.

presets.label: RX 6500 XT 8GB
presets.note: RDNA 2, so prompt processing is capped by the silicon: these cards have no matrix cores at all — llama.cpp enables WMMA only on RDNA 3 and newer. Generation is bandwidth-bound and barely affected. ROCm has never supported this GPU target in any release — not with an override either. Vulkan is the path, and it is a good one. Also a 64-bit bus on a PCIe x4 link — 144GB/s is the lowest here, and the narrow link makes any spill to system RAM worse than usual. A warning rather than an option. On AMD, prefer llama.cpp's Vulkan backend (RADV) over ROCm for generation: across llama.cpp's own scoreboards Vulkan leads token generation on every AMD chip measured. Prompt processing is split between the two.

presets.label: RX 6800 XT 16GB
presets.note: RDNA 2, and that decides its prompt processing. These cards have no matrix cores at all — llama.cpp's amd_wmma_available() is true only for RDNA 3 and newer, and RDNA 2 falls back to dp4a; Mesa's RADV likewise exposes cooperative matrix only on GFX11 and up. So the ceiling on reading a long prompt is set by the silicon, not by a driver that might improve. It is the honest reason a cheap 6800 XT is not simply a cheap 7800 XT. Generating tokens, which is bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound, is much less affected — this card's 512GB/s is real. runtimeOverhead.note: A running model needs more than weights and KV cache, and what it needs is knowable rather than a rule of thumb. Three terms, each derived from what llama.cpp allocates for one micro-batch: the final vocabulary projection (ubatch x vocabSize x 4 bytes), the peak live activations through the FFN (activationCopies x ubatch x width x 4), and the KQ mask, which is the only part that grows with context (context x ubatch x 2). The mechanism is checkable: llama.cpp's own documented example is a 507MB compute buffer for Gemma 2 9B, and 512 x 256000 x 4 is 500MB — the vocabulary projection IS the compute buffer, to within 1.4 percent, with nothing fitted. This replaced a term of the form 'baseGb + 6 percent of weights', which used the wrong variable entirely: it charged a 397B mixture-of-experts 15.6GB of scratch and a model a third as wide three times more than a wider one. Parameter count does not size a compute buffer; vocabulary, width and batch do. Only frameworkGb is not derived — published figures put llama.cpp plus its backend kernels at 0.5-1.5GB — so the estimate is a range, and fit verdicts take the pessimistic end. NOT YET CHECKED AGAINST A REAL MACHINE. An earlier note claimed corroboration from a measured ~80K context on a 32GB Mac; that reading was taken with the wired limit raised, so it was never a 24GB-budget measurement and could not test this. The claim has been withdrawn rather than reworded. See docs/measuring-runtime-overhead.md for how to produce a reading that would actually test it.

systemMemory.label: DDR4, 2 channels (older desktop or laptop)
systemMemory.note: DDR4-3200 in the two channels a mainstream board has: 3200 x 8 bytes x 2. The floor for anything built before roughly 2022, and the reason an older machine offloads noticeably worse than a current one with the same graphics card.

systemMemory.label: DDR5, 2 channels (current desktop or laptop)
systemMemory.note: DDR5-5600 in two channels: 5600 x 8 bytes x 2 = 89.6GB/s. What almost every desktop and laptop sold now has, and the default here for that reason.

systemMemory.label: DDR5, 2 channels, all four slots filled
systemMemory.note: Still two channels, but clocked down: a desktop memory controller that runs DDR5-5600 across two DIMMs drops to about DDR5-3600 across four. 3600 x 8 bytes x 2 = 57.6GB/s. This is the trap in maxing out a consumer board for local models — going from 96GB to 192GB by filling the empty slots costs roughly 36% of your memory bandwidth, and on a machine with no graphics card that is 36% of your tokens per second. Twice the model, two thirds the speed.

systemMemory.label: DDR5, 4 channels (workstation)

systemMemory.label: DDR5, 8 channels (Threadripper PRO)

systemMemory.label: DDR5, 12 channels (EPYC / Xeon server)
systemMemory.note: Twelve channels of DDR5-4800: 4800 x 8 bytes x 12 = 460.8GB/s. Newer server parts run faster still; this is the conservative reading of the generation.

perTokenLatency.note: The part of a token's cost that does not scale with weight bytes — kernel launches, attention over the KV cache, sampling, expert routing — charged PER LAYER, in milliseconds. Time per token is bytes-read/bandwidth plus layers x this. Solved from published measurements, not assumed. Per-layer rather than per-token because a flat per-token figure does not hold: it comes to 6-14ms on a 32-layer 7B and 25-41ms on an 80-layer 70B, and divided by layer count both land in the same few tenths of a millisecond, which is what a per-layer kernel dispatch would do. Per platform because it does not transfer. The discrete figure is CUDA-derived (an 8B at 4-bit on an RTX 4090: 85-125 tok/s measured, 86-124 predicted) and AMD and Intel sit inside it, which is likely optimistic for them. The unified figure is set from 92 published Apple Silicon decode measurements attributed to a named chip, across llama.cpp and MLX (docs/mac-tok-s-validation.md). Solved for the overhead each implies at peak bandwidth: llama.cpp's 2023 table (the citation) 0.12-0.22 on dense models; 2026 llama.cpp builds 0.05-0.15 dense and 0.10-0.31 mixture-of-experts; MLX 0.02-0.13 dense and 0.09-0.30 mixture-of-experts. The range is wide because the overhead is not one number: expert routing costs 2-3x a dense layer, and a current build dispatches about half as expensively as the 2023 one. 0.05-0.30 brackets 76 of the 92 (llama.cpp 42 of 48, MLX 34 of 44); what escapes is dense MLX on M3 Ultra and M4 chips at 0.02-0.04, up to a tenth past the top of the range, and prompts of 15K tokens or more, where attention over the cache pushes it below. The previous unified figure, 0.21-0.45, was fitted to Llama-3.3-70B on an M2 Ultra including a Q2_K row, and Q2_K is compute-bound in dequantisation; it left 75 of the 92 measurements above the range. Before that this was a multiplicative 45-70% 'fraction of peak bandwidth'. That was the wrong shape: utilisation is not something an engine has, it is what you see when a fixed overhead is divided by a varying read. It is why 4-bit looks less efficient than F16 on the same chip, and why sparse mixture-of-experts models were overpredicted by roughly two times — they read little per token, so the overhead dominates and a bandwidth fraction flatters them. The default spans both platforms and is what a platform with no measurements of its own gets.
